THE  BEST  FOR  EVERYBODY 

BECAUSE 

It  is  easy  to  find  the  word  wanted. 

Words  are  given  their  correct  alphabetical  places  in  the 
vocabulary,  rarh  one  begining  a  paragraph  so  as  to  be  readily 
caught  by  the  eye. 

It  is  easy  to  ascertain  the  pronunciation. 

The  pronunciation  is  indicated  by  the  ordinary  diacritically  marked  letters  used  in 
the  schoolbooks,  whose  sounds  are  taught  in  the  public  schools. 

It  is  easy  to  trace  the  growth  of  a  word. 

The  etymologies  are  complete  and  scientific,  and  the  different  meanings  a  word  has 
acquired  are  given  in  the  order  of  their  growth  from  the  root  idea. 

It  is  easy  to  learn  what  a  word  means. 

The  definitions  arc  dear,  explicit,  and  full;  terse,  yet  comprehensive.    Each  defi- 
nition is  contained  in  a,  separate  paragraph.

Our  prices  are  lower  than  the  lowest,  and  supplying  Y.  M.  C.  A.  Heading-Rooms  our

If  Secretaries  or  Reading  Room  Committees  will  forward  us  a  list  of  such  publications  as 
wanted,  we  will  make  an  estimate  of  coat,  below  anything  they  have  from  others,  and 
promptly  return  with  other  special  features. 

Our  arrangements  are  such  that  we  supply  to  our  patrons  complimentary  copies  of  many 
such  new  publications,  as  they  appear,  as  aie  worthy  the  patronage  of  Associations. 

We  supply  many  Associations,  to  whom  we  will  gladly  refer  you  when  asked.

CAST-STEEL    WORKS 

OF 

FRIED.    KRUPP,    Essen,    Germany. 

AMERICAN  OFFICE,  15  GOLD  STREET,  NEW  YORK. 

P.  O.  Box,  2878. 
Represented  by   THOMAS   PROSSER  &  SON. 

These  works  cover  an  area  of  1,200  acres,  employ  about  30,000  ineii,  have  the  must 
improved  plant ,  and  stand  unique,  from  the  fact  that  they  have  their  own  Ore  and  Coal 
Mines,  JBlast  Furnaces,  etc  ,  aud  that  every  stage  of  manufacture  is  under  their  own  super- 
vision, and  are  not  (like  others*  dependent  on  the  open  market  for  a  miscellaneous  assort- 
ment of  crude  material,  which,  in  connection  with  15  years'  experience,  enables  them  to 
turn  out  a  product  of  very  superior  quality,  second  to  none,  and  at  the  same  time  the 
different  grades  of  Steel  are  always  of  the  same  uniform  quality. 

LOCOMOTIVE   TIRES,  STEEL  TIRED  WHEELS,  AXLES,  CRANK 

PINS,  SHAFTS  AND  STEEL  FORCINGS  UP  TO  70  TONS. 
Steel  of  every  description  Forged,  Rolled,  etc.,  into  any  form  or  article  desired. 


After  a  test  of  over  35  years,  the  "KRUPP  TIRE"  has  proved  itself  to  be  the 
best  in  the  market,  and  parties  intending  ordering  Locomotives  would  do  well  to  insert  in 
their  specifications  that  "  KRUPP  TIRES"  be  used  on  drivers,  and  thereby  obtain 
an  article  which  will  give  satisfaction.

(PEN-WRITTEN    COPIES  .Reproduced.) 

The  Books  enumerated  above  are  especially  adapted  for  use  in  Y.  M.  C.  A.  Educational 
Classes.     This  is  particularly  true  of  the 


owing  to  the  method  employed  in  presenting  and  treating  the  subject.  By  this  method 
the  pupil  is  initiated  into  the  science  in  an  easy  natural  and  fascinating  way,  and  with 
little  or  no  assistance  from  the  teacher.  The  work  which  the  pupil  is  required  to  do  is 
of  the  most 

PRACTICAL    CHARACTER, 

and  is  so  arranged  that  his  progress  depends  entirely  on  his  own  ability  and  the  time  he 
devotes  to  the  subject.  By  the  use  of  varied  price  lists,  original  with  the  method,  results 
obtained  by  each  one  of  several  pupils  are  different  from  the  others,  thus  preventing  pupils 
from  copying  or  getting  assistance  from  one  another,  while  at  the  same  time  it 

DEVELOPS    ACCURACY    AND    SELF-RELIANCE. 

As  no  class  work  is  necessary  by  this  method,  the  labor  of  a  teacher  is  reduced  to  the 
minimum,  and  consists  chiefly  in  examining  the  pupils'  work  and  rendering  them  such 
assistance  individually  aa  they  may  require  to  obtain  accurate  results. 

The  introduction  of  this  system  of  bookkeeping  is  greatly  facilitated  by  the 

TEACHERS'  REFERENCE  BOOK  AND  TEACHERS'  KEY, 

a  copy  of  each  of  which  is  supplied  to  Associations  adopting  the  work.  The  Reference 
Book  contains  all  of  the  entries  which  the  pupils  make  in  their  books,  and  the  key 
contains  their  results,  which  are  arrranged  in  convenient  form  for  quick  and  easy  ref«rence. 
Among  the 

ASSOCIATIONS    THAT    HAVE    ADOPTED 

this  system  of  bookkeeping  may  be  mentioned  the  following:  New  York,  Chicago, 
Baltimore,  Washington,  Detroit,  Providence,  Hartford,  and  Atlanta. 
An  examination  of  the  work  will  convince  any  progressive  teacher  of  its  superior  merits. 


Specimen  panes  of  any  of  the  above  publications  and  illustrated  catalogue  will  be  sent  free 
to  Association  officers  and  teachers. 


WILLIAMS  &  ROGERS, 

PUBLISHERS, 
Y.  M,  C.  A.  Building,  ROCHESTER,  N.  Y.          Caxton  Building,  CHICAGO,  ILL 

MENTION    YEAR    BOOK. 


In  a  recent  address  at  the  University 
of  Chicago,  Mr.  Depew  in  commenting 
on    the  well  known    fact  that   a   large 
majority  of  our  Presidents,  Cabinet  Minis- 
ters, Congressmen,  Governors  and  Legisla- 
tors have  been  lawyers,  very  forcibly  said, 
the  reason  for  this  was  not  because  lawyers 
are  better  lawmakers  than  farmers  or  business 
men,   but  because   the  lawyers   have  been  better  trained. 
Here  is  a  point  worthy  the  most  serious  thought  by 
those   who  wish   to  do  better.     The  study  of  law  not  only 
fits   one  for  the  profitable  practice  of    that  profession,  but  it 
gives  him    marked    advantage  over   his  fellows  whatever  may 
be   his  walk  in  life. 

This  sounds  well  you  say:  Yes,  and  it  is  well.  More  than  3000 
men  and  woim-n  have  studied  law  at  home  with  us  and  proved  it 
true ;  and  the  starting  point  with  every  one  was  a  postal  or  letter 
to  us,  requesting  particulars  just  such  as  you  may  write  to-day. 

We  are  the  originators  and  perfectors  of  this  system  of  self- 
improvement,  and  it  is  a  settled  success.  The  work  is  done  by  mail, 
and  location  is,  therefore,  no  obstacle  to  you  or  us.  You  can  receive 
the  benefit  of  all  our  advantages  right  where  you  are,  and  that  at  no 
more  outlay  than  it  would  cost  you  for  something  said  to  be  the  same, 
but  like  ours  only  in  name. 

Who  our  students  are,  what  they  had  to  do,  the  cost  and  much 
other  useful  information  will  be  sent  you  without  charge  on  receipt 
of  your  address.     If  you  wish  to  do  better  here  is  a  way — and  a  postal,, 
card  will  open  it  to-day  if  you  will  mail  it  to 
Till.   SPRAOTT.  CORRESPONDENCE    vSCHOOL  OF  LAW, 
85  TKIMIK.M    Hni.niNi;,   DETROIT,   MICH.

STATEMENT    EEGAEDING    THE    WORK    OF    THE 
INTEKNATIONAL    COMMITTEE. 

I.  — The  regular  monthly  meetings  of  the  Committee  and  its  eight  sub- 
committees have  been  held  as  reported  in  previous  years. 

A  conference  of  the  Committee  and  its  secretaries  was  held  at  Pough- 
keepsie,  N.  Y.,  August  29  to  September  2,  1805,  when  all  branches  of  the 
international  work  were  carefully  reviewed,  with  reference  to  their  devel- 
opment during  the  coming  year. 

The  annual  dinner  meeting  of  the  Committee  and  its  friends  in  New 
York,  November  21,  was  more  largely  attended  and  effective  than  any  of 
its  predecessors.  Similar  meetings  were  held  in  Manchester,  N.  H., 
October  21,  Chicago  November  5  and  Cleveland  November  7. 

The  Board  of  Trustees  held  its  annual  meeting  April  26,  1895,  at  which 
the  officers  of  the  preceding  year  were  re-elected. 

II. — In  response  to  the  usual  requests  for  such  co-operation,  representa- 
tives of  the  Committee  participated  in  thirty-four  State  and  Provincial 
Conventions  during  1895.  Their  names  are  given  elsewhere,  in  the  table 
of  these  gatherings.  Many  expressions  of  thanks  have  been  received  for 
the  aid  thus  rendered.  For  thirty  years  the  Committee  has  given  steadily 
growing  attention  to  this  form  of  service,  with  increasing  evidence  of  its 
conferring  great  benefit,  not  only  in  the  form  of  the  immediate  help  ren- 
dered, but  also  because  of  its  happy  influence  in  strengthening  the  ties 
which  unite  the  Associations  in  one  brotherhood  and  in  emphasizing  the 
fundamental  principles  and  the  best  tested  methods,  old  and  new,  in  the 
work. 

It  is,  however,  a  very  perplexing  matter  to  administer,  because  so  many 
conventions  meet  on  the  same  day,  and  often  urge  the  presence  of  the 
same  men  at  points  hundreds  of  miles  apart. 

III. — Robert  Weidensall,  the  honored  senior  secretary  of  the  Committee, 
has  continued  his  life  work,  devoting  to  it  such  time  as  his  private  affairs 
have  allowed,  and  at  nominal  expense  to  the  Committee.  He  has  labored 
chiefly  in  the  states  of  South  Carolina,  Maryland,  West  Virginia,  Ken- 
tucky and  Minnesota.  The  county  work,  which  has  made  decided 
progress  through  his  vigorous  efforts,  has  been  his  chief  care. 

IV. — Territorial  Administration.  As  outlined  at  the  International  Con- 
vention at  Springfield,  and  in  accordance  with  its  instructions,  the 


10 

continent  has  been  divided  into  several  sections.  In  as  many  of  these  as 
the  present  resources  of  the  Committee  permit  an  international  field 
secretary  has  been  stationed,  charged  to  render  such  aid  to  the  local  and 
state  work  as  may  be  requisite  and  practicable.  His  residence  near  the 
points  where  help  is  needed  renders  possible  a  speedy  and  intelligent 
response  to  such  calls. 

Upon  this  plan  of  work  C.  K.  Ober,  who  suggested  the  plan  and 
through  whom  the  Committee  has  carried  out  many  of  its  details,  with 
headquarters  in  Chicago,  has  rendered  valuable  aid  in  the  section  of  which 
that  city  is  the  natural  center,  and  has  visited  the  Pacific  Coast.  He 
has  maintained  a  relation  of  counsel  and  help  toward  the  other  field 
secretaries,  and  has  been  active  in  securing  funds  to  carry  on  this  branch 
of  the  work.  He  has  also  sustained  a  close  relation  to  the  growing  work 
among  Indian  young  men. 

H.  P.  Andersen  and  C.  L.  Gates  have  continued  their  labors  in  the 
South  and  Southwest. 

In  September  W.  B.  Millar  became  a  field  secretary  of  the  Committee, 
with  headquarters  in  New  York  City,  his  work  relating  specially  to  the 
region  between  Nova  Scotia  and  West  Virginia. 

During  portions  of  1895  C.  M.  Copeland  and  C.  S.  Ward,  as  special 
agents  of  the  Committee,  rendered  valuable  aid  in  Manitoba,  North  and 
South  Dakota,  Nebraska  and  Minnesota.  At  the  opening  of  1896  Mr. 
Copeland  entered  the  service  of  the  Committee,  as  one  of  its  secretaries, 
with  special  reference  to  this  field. 

The  field  secretaries  have  aided  state  work  (1)  by  temporarily  taking 
charge  of  state  work  that  has  suffered  disaster;  (2)  by  counseling  state 
committees  about  desirable  men  for  them  to  employ;  (3)  by  uniting  two 
or  more  states  unable  alone  to  support  a  state  secretary  in  the  employ- 
ment of  one  man;  (4)  by  aiding  in  securing  money  for  state  work;  (5)  by 
arranging  for  and  participating  in  state  conventions  in  fields  where  no 
state  secretary  is  employed;  (6)  by  hearty  participation  in  other  state 
conventions  and  conferences  ;  (7)  by  helping  state  committees  and  secre- 
taries in  special  emergencies;  (8)  by  suggesting  forms  of  work  already 
undertaken  successfully  elsewhere;  (9)  by  stimulating  to  broader  and 
more  aggressive  efforts;  U0>  by  helping  to  guard  against  dangerous 
tendencies. 

In  similar  ways  they  have  assisted  many  local  Associations. 

Several  of  them  also  co-operated  with  Mr.  D.  L  Moody,  at  his  request, 
in  managing  an  Association  camp  for  young  men  at  Northfield,  Mass., 
during  July  and  August,  1895. 

V. — Departmental  work. — 1.  George  B.  Hodge  has  continued  his  unre- 
mitting efforts  in  behalf  of  the  Educational  Department.  He  visited  dur- 
ing the  year  important  Associations  from  Nova  Scotia  to  British  Columbia, 
and  from  Georgia  to  Texas  and  Southern  California.  The  portable 
exhibit,  showing  results  of  evening  class  work  in  various  Associations, 
together  with  Mr.  Hodge's  vivid  presentation  of  the  practical  value  and 
methods  of  such  work,  led  many  of  these  Associations  to  undertake  it 
with  far  more  energy  and  system.  Forty  Associations  organized  educa- 
tional work  for  the  first  time  this  year ;  the  evening  classes  have  had  a 


11 

membership  of  23,000,  being  2,500  more  than  ever  before  ;  and  the  con- 
stantly improving  quality  of  the  work  done  has  both  directly  and  indi- 
rectly increased  the  membership  of  the  Associations,  raised  their  stand- 
ing in  their  comunities,  and  enlarged  their  financial  constituency. 

The  exhibit  at  the  International  Convention  last  May,  while  one  of 
hope  rather  than  large  achievement,  greatly  surpassed  any  former  exhibit. 
Awards  of  merit  were  given  for  the  first  time  and  have  proved  a  powerful 
stimulus  to  better  work. 

The  great  lack  of  printed  matter  on  this  subject  has  been  partially  sup- 
plied by  the  issue  of  various  record  blanks  and  pamphlets.  Another 
new  measure  is  the  examination  offered  by  the  Committee  for  the  first 
time  this  spring  in  arithmetic  and  mechanical  drawing. 

2.  The  chief  forward  step  in  the  Physical  Department  has  been  the 
organization  of  the    Athletic  League    of  the    Young  Men's    Christian 
Associations  of  North  America.     On  the  basis  of  plans  and  preparations 
made  during  several  previous  years,  and  after  careful  consideration,  the 
Springfield  Convention  recommended  this  organization.     Eighty  Asso- 
ations  have  joined  the  League.     They  have  52,000  members,  or  over  one- 
fifth  of  the  membership  of  all  the  Associations. 

Its  objects,  as  stated  in  its  constitution,  are  :  (1)  The  furtherance 
of  Association  physical  department  work  ;  (2)  the  institution,  regulation 
and  government  of  inter-association  gymnastic  and  athletic  meets  of  all 
kinds  ;  (3i  the  securing  and  maintenance  of  a  genuine  amateur  basis  in 
Association  sport. 

It  will  aim  to  promote  not  merely  the  interests  of  sport,  but  the  best 
physical  development  of  men,  in  order  to  increase  their  spiritual  and 
intellectual  efficiency.  Dr.  Luther  Gulick  is  secretary  of  the  League. 
George  W.  Ehler,  of  Chicago,  is  co-operating  in  its  work  in  that  section 
of  the  country. 

3.  Among  the  encouraging  features  in  the  College  Department  are  the 
increase  of  the  college  Associations  to  over  500  in  number,  many  of  the 
new  organizations  being  in  professional  colleges — hitherto  altogether  the 
most  difficult  to  reach  ;    the  enrollment  of  8,000  students  in  voluntary 
Bible  classes  and  the  hopeful  conversion  of  over  3,000  ;  and  the  growing 
efficiency  of  the  conferences  of  College  Association  presidents  and  of 
the  three  summer  schools  in  which  the   student  leaders  of   the  work 
receive  practical  training  for  it.     To  the  three  schools  a  fourth  is  to  be 
added,  in  response  to  urgent  request  of  students  on  the  Pacific  Coast. 

John  K.  Mott  started  in  June  on  a  tour  of  visitation  and  attendance 
at  conferences  in  Europe,  Asia  and  Australia,  with  the  object  of  pro- 
moting Christian  life  among  students.  Remarkable  success  has  crowned 
the  effort.  The  tour  is  made  without  expense  to  the  Committee's 
treasury. 

During  his  absence  F.  S.  Brockman,  in  addition  to  extensive  visitation 
among  colleges  chiefly  in  the  South,  is  acting  chairman  of  the  executive 
committee  of  the  Student  Volunteer  Movement. 

Gilbert  A.  Beaver  and  C.  C.  Michener,  who  had  previously  rendered 
valuable  service  as  special  agents  in  the  college  field,  became  college 
secretaries  of  the  Committee  September  1st. 


12 

At  the  same  time  H.  W.  Georgi  took  charge  of  the  office  work  of  the 
college  department,  succeeding  C.  S.  Cooper.  Much  of  the  success  of 
the  department  is  due  to  the  quiet,  energetic  work  at  the  central  office. 

Mr.  Beaver  has  visited  Eastern  colleges.  Mr.  Michener  has  made  the 
annual  tour  among  the  colleges  in  the  Far  West  and  upon  the  Pacific 
Coast,  and  held  five  very  profitable  conferences  of  students  at  Los  Angeles 
and  Berkeley,  California;  Eugene,  Oregon;  Tacoma,  Washington;  and 
Moscow,  Idaho.  The  last  named  was  the  first  gathering  of  this  descrip- 
tion ever  held  for  Idaho,  eastern  Oregon  and  eastern  Washington. 

4.  C.  J.  Hicks  and  E.  L.  Hamilton  have  pushed  the  work  of  the  Kail- 
road  Department.  In  September  H.  O.  Williams  became  their  associate. 
Through  visitation  and  a  careful  system  of  quarterly  reports  from  all  the 
Railroad  Associations,  they  have  kept  in  close  touch  with  the  field. 
Much  communication  has  also  been  maintained  with  railroad  officials, 
whose  support  of  the  work  is  now  more  hearty  than  ever  before.  In 
several  cases  where  railroad  managers  were  considering  the  reduction  or 
withdrawal  of  appropriations,  a  full  presentation  of  the  work  has  led  to 
their  continuance. 

Eight  Associations  have  been  added  to  the  list  during  the  year  :  Con- 
cord, N.  H.  ;  Camden,  N.  J.  ;  Rouse's  Point  and  Utica,  N.  Y.  ;  Dennison 
and  Youngstown,  Ohio  ;  Bellwood,  Pa. ;  and  Indianapolis,  at  Brightwood. 
At  Minneapolis  the  Railroad  Department  has  been  discontinued,  and  at 
Plattsburgh,  N.  Y. ,  it  has  been  reorganized  into  a  city  Association.  The 
total  number  of  Railroad  Associations  is  now  109. 

Considerable  time  has  been  spent  in  preparation  for  new  organizations 
at  several  division  points,  including  Fitchburg,  Mass.;  New  Haven, 
Conn.,  and  Russell,  Ky. 

Cecil  L.  Gates  has  spent  a  month  at  Pocatello,  Idaho,  re-establishing 
the  work  for  railroad  men,  which  had  been  discontinued  for  a  year.  This 
effort  was  made  possible  through  the  "Sidney  Dillon  Fund,"  the  income 
of  which  is  devoted  to  work  among  the  employees  of  the  Union  Pacific 
Railroad. 

At  St.  Louis,  where  the  finest  railroad  station  in  the  world  has  recently 
been  opened,  the  committee  is  co-operating  with  the  local  Association  in 
securing  a  building  for  the  use  of  the  3,700  railroad  men.  The  Terminal 
Company  has  leased  to  the  St.  Louis  Association,  at  a  nominal  rental,  a 
piece  of  land  immediately  adjoining  the  station,  that  cost  the  company 
825,000.  The  Terminal  Company  agrees  to  furnish,  without  charge, 
steam  heat  and  electric  light  for  the  building.  Plans  have  been  prepared 
for  a  building  to  cost  875,000.  The  expense  of  erecting  and  maintaining 
it  will  be  borne  by  the  railroad  companies  using  the  station  in  the  same 
way  as  the  expense  of  the  station  itself. 

The  Kansas  City  Railroad  Association  has  received  considerable  atten- 
tion from  the  Committee,  and  the  work  at  that  point  is  in  a  very  promis- 
ing condition. 

Since  April,  J.  M.  Burwick,  a  freight  conductor  from  the  Evansville 
and  Terre  Haute  Railroad,  has  been  promoting  Bible  study  and  holding 
evangelistic  meetings  among  railroad  men,  under  direction  of  the  Com- 
mittee. He  has  spent  from  one  to  two  weeks  at  each  point,  and  has 


13 

reached  large  numbers  of  his  fellow  railroad  men  and  led  them  to  Christ. 
The  necessary  expense  has  been  borne  entirely  by  the  Associations  visited. 

The  eighth  railroad  conference  was  held  at  Clifton  Forge,  Va.,  Sep- 
tember 13-15,  1895,  with  the  unusually  large  attendance  of  469  delegates. 
It  was  by  far  the  best  of  the  series,  being  specially  remarkable  for  its  high 
spiritual  tone. 

The  total  mileage  of  roads  now  contributing  to  the  support  of  railroad 
departments  on  their  lines  is  over  100,000  miles,  or  about  50  per  cent, 
of  the  entire  railroad  mileage  in  North  America. 

5.  Claus  Olandt,  Jr. ,  has  devoted  about  one-third  of  the  past  year  to 
work  among  German-speaking  young  men.     The  rest  of  his  time  has  been 
spent  in  the  service  of  the  State  Committee  of  Vermont  and  New  Hamp- 
shire, and  without  expense  to  the  treasury  of  the  International  Com- 
mittee. 

6.  W.  A.  Hunton  has  visited  most  of  the  Associations  of  colored  men, 
both  in  cities  and  colleges,  bringing  to  them  much  encouragement  and 
help.     Two  deeply  spiritual  and  practical  conferences  of  these  Associa- 
tions at  Richmond,  Ya. ,  and  Atlanta,  Ga. ,  were  attended  by  sixty  repre- 
sentative delegates  from  seven  States. 

7.  Forty-three  Associations  of  Indian  young  men  have  been  organized 
on  the  reservations  and  in  the  training  schools.    Dr.  C.  A.  Eastman,  one 
of  their  own  race,  a  graduate  of  Dartmouth  College  and  of  the  Boston 
Medical  School,  has  labored  earnestly  and  successfully  for  the  develop- 
ment of  these  Associations. 

VI. — The  Central  Office.  The  office  secretaries  find  that  the  demands 
upon  them  become  more  and  more  taxing  with  the  growing  complexity 
of  the  field  work.  The  securing  of  competent  men  as  secretaries  and 
physical  directors  becomes  more  difficult  as  the  standard  of  their  quali- 
fications is  raised.  Thirty  new  pamphlets  and  leaflets  have  been  issued. 
The  number  of  contributions  for  the  work  of  the  Committee  has  increased 
of  recent  years.  Each  new  gift  takes  time  for  its  solicitation,  record  and 
acknowledgment.  Messrs.  Cree  and  Lougee  have  done  much  in  this  line 
of  work,  and  have  also  rendered  frequent  financial  help  to  local  Associa- 
tions. 

The  gifts  of  the  Associations  and  of  individuals  to  the  international 
treasury  have  been  as  follows  : 

1894.  1895. 

From  Association  treasuries $3,462  33       $6,047  74 

"      extension  funds 1,422  74          1,141  87 

"     Week  of  Prayer  collections 4,341  06          3,471  23 

$9,226  13      $10,660  84 
"      individuals 53,598  83        54,484  86 


$62,824  96      $65,145  70 

The  first  item  shows  a  gratifying  advance,  due  probably  to  special  ap- 
peals to  the  Associations,  authorized  by  the  Springfield  Convention.  But 
unfortunately  this  advance  is  accompanied  by  a  decrease  in  the  other  two 


14 

forms  in  which  the  Associations  contribute,  so  that  the  total  of  direct  and 
indirect  gifts  from  the  Associations  themselves  is  only  $1,434.71  more  in 
1895  than  in  1894,  and  is  32,617.26  less  than  in  1893.  The  total  number  of 
Associations  contributing  in  one  or  more  forms  varied  from  680  in  1893  to 
557  in  1894,  and  540  in  1895.  Every  one  familiar  with  the  financial  matters 
of  a  local  Association  can  understand  the  difficulty  of  conducting  the 
work  of  the  Committee  under  such  variations  of  resources  from  year  to 
year. 

The  resignation  of  P.  Augustus  Weiting,  rendered  necessary  by  the  con- 
dition of  his  health,  was  accepted  with  great  regret  in  November.  Mr. 
Wieting  entered  the  office  of  the  Committee  in  1879  and  had  rendered 
efficient  service  in  every  department  of  the  office  work. 

The  Historical  Library  has  grown  as  usual,  under  the  care  of  J.  T. 
Bowne. 

The  observance  of  the  Day  and  "Week  of  Prayer  in  November  resulted 
in  great  good  to  multitudes  of  young  men.  The  Committee  and  its  sec- 
retaries made  special  effort  in  its  promotion. 

VII. — The  Foreign  Work.  1.  Good  progress  has  been  made  upon  the 
foreign  field. 

The  Association  building  in  Tokyo  has  become  the  recognized  rallying 
center  of  many  important  Christian  and  philanthropic  movements.  J.  T. 
Swift  returned  from  America  to  that  city  in  October,  fully  restored  to 
health. 

B.  S.  Miller,  Jr  ,  with  the  concurrence  of  the  Committee,  accepted  the 
position  of  interpreter  for  the  United  States  Legation  in  September,  1895. 
This  government  position  has  been  held  in  former  years  by  missionaries 
expert  in  this  difficult  language,  for,  while  thus  earning  their  own  support 
during  the  period  of  their  service,  the  official  duties  of  the  position  have 
not  prevented  them  from  continuing  active  in  Christian  work.  In  fact, 
the  holding  of  the  position  has  often  made  their  Christian  work  more 
effective  and  influential.  Similar  good  results  the  Committee  expects  will 
follow  in  the  case  of  Mr.  Miller. 

David  McConaughy,  Jr.,  has  been  engaged  in  securing  in  America  the 
money  to  erect  a  building  in  Madras  on  the  excellent  site  purchased 
through  the  generosity  of  friends  in  Great  Britain.  Raymond  J.  Davis 
has  been  in  charge  of  the  Madras  Association.  After  a  year's  successful 
effort  in  developing  the  Association  among  young  business  men,  J. 
Campbell  White  has  begun  in  another  part  of  Calcutta  a  work  among 
the  ten  thousand  students  of  that  city. 

The  Association  in  Rio  de  Janeiro  has  grown  under  the  secretaryship  of 
Myron  A.  Clark.  Two  other  Associations  have  been  organized  in  Brazil. 

D.  Willard  Lyon  reached  China  in  October.    After  carefully  studying 

I   openings  he  decided  to  settle  for  the  present  in  Tientsin,  an 

important  student  center.     An  Association  numbering  seventy,  chiefly 

composed  of  English  -speaking  students,  was  organized  soon  after  his 

arrival,  and  has  already  made  remarkable  progress. 

L.  D.  Wishard  was  granted  a  leave  of  absence  last  July  and  accompan- 
ied Mr.  M-  MIL lent  Conferences  of  Great  Britain,  Germany  and 
mavia.  The  principal  object  of  his  absence  was  to  visit  South 


15 

Africa  in  the  interest  of  the  Association  work ;  but  the  condition  of  his 
own  and  of  Mrs.  Wishard'sh  ealth  was  such  that  he  experienced  unex- 
pected detention  during  the  autumn  and  winter,  and  is  to  undertake 
in  the  present  year  the  African  visitation  which  he  had  expected  to  ac- 
complish in  1895. 

VIII. — The  International  Convention,  held  at  Springfield,  Mass.,  May 
8-12,  1895,  was  a  great  meeting  in  size,  in  the  representative  character  of 
its  delegates  and  in  the  attention  given  to  new  and  growing  features  of 
the  work.  Allusion  has  already  been  made  to  some  of  its  results.  In 
many  other  ways  it  aroused  and  quickened  intelligent  interest  in  both  the 
home  and  the  foreign  work. 

EICHARD  C.  MORSE, 

General  Secretary.

have  building  funds  paid  in  amounting  to  $7,i90,  and  four  Departments  own  other  real  estate  valued 
at  $16,200. 

At  the  following  points  entire  buildings  are  set  aside  for  the  use  of  the  Railroad  Department  by 
railroad  companies  or  officials :

TION TRAINING  SCHOOL,  Springfield,  Mass. 

EQUIPMENT:  DORMITORY  Building  containing  Lecture  Hall  seating  300,  Chem- 
cal,  Physical  and  Physiological  Laboratories.  Recitation  Rooms.  Libraries,  Offices,  Reception 
and  Social  Rooms,  Dormitories,  and  on  the  fourth  floor  a  Kitchen  and  Dining  Hall. 

GYMNASIUM  with  floor  48x74,  free  from  posts,  contains  the  usual  apparatus,  and  in  addi- 
tion Swedish  boms,  hand-ball  court,  class  climbing  ropes,  seven  needle  baths  with  hot  and 
cold  water,  lockers  with  combination  locks,  workshops,  class  rooms,  examining  room,  phys- 
ical department  library  containing  nine  hundred  and  forty-five  books  and  pamphlets  on 
physical  training  and  allied  subjects. 

ATHLETIC  GROUNDS  with  quarter-mile  track,  grand  stand,  bicycle  ahed.  tennis  courts, 
foot  ball  field,  rings  for  hammer  throw,  etc.,  etc.  Lake  bordering  on  school  grounds  for 
aquatics,  boats  and  canoes  on  Connecticut  River  for  practice  in  rowing  and  paddling. 

COURSE  OF  INSTRUCTION.—  This  covers  three  years,  and  includes  the  fol- 
lowing subjects  taught  with  special  reference  to  their  application  to  Association  work  : 

THE  BIBLE.  —  The  synthetic  study  of  both  the  Old  and  New  Testament  Scriptures, 
history  of  the  Bible,  covering  authorship,  composition,  and  the  authority  of  the  books,  princi- 
ples of  interpretation,  practical  use  and  application  of  Scripture  teaching,  together  with 
lessons  for  the  personal  worker.  Also  short  courses  on  the  evidences  of  Christianity  and 
outlines  of  church  history. 

jJIAN.—  His  threefold  nature,  his  education  or  the  means  of  his  development,  and  his 
relationships,  including  (1)  the  study  of  Physics,  Chemistry,  Biology,  Anatomy,  Physiology. 
Hygiene,  Physical  Measurement,  Personal  Purity,  First  Aid  to  the  Injured,  Physiology. 
(2)  Pedagogy  or  the  Art  of  Instruction,  with  special  reference  to  the  educational  work  of  the 
Associations.  (3)  Ethics  and  Sociology,  including  the  study  of  social  forces  and  social  prob- 
lems from  aa  historical  standpoint,  with  the  underlying  principles  involved  in  their  solution 
and  the  relation  of  the  Association  to  such  problems. 

THE  YOUNG  UIEN'S  CHRISTIAN  ASSOCIATION.  -Its  history,  field, 
scope,  methods,  its  several  departments,  and  its  business  management,  with  special  emphasis 
on  the  duties  and  relations  of  its  employed  officers 

PRACTICE.—  Practice  is  required  of  all  students,  in  gymnastics,  athletics,  aquatics, 
and  in  forming  and  conducting  athletic  and  gymnastic  organizations,  gymnasium  exhibi- 
tions. etc.  Individual  work  is  done  in  the  physical,  chemical,  physiological,  and  mechanical 
laboratories.  The  students  have  a  part  in  all  the  regular  work  of  the  local  Young  Men's 
Christian  Association  and  the  neighboring  Associations.  They  also  participate  in  the  literary 
and  other  school  societies.  Observation  tours  are  made  to  scientific  aud  industrial  institutions. 


Send  for  Catalogue  to  Oliver  C  Morse,  Corresponding  Secretary.

HALL'S    FAC-SIMILE    PRESS. 


NEW     YORK,     May    1st,  1896, 

Mr.    Reid    Itthroo, 

211  Rush   St. , 

Businessville. 
Dear  Sin- 
Has  it  ever  occurred  to  you  that  the  most 
direct  way  to  reach  the  people  whose  trade  you 
seek  is  to  send  them  a  personal  letter?  You  can 
be  assured  it  is  always  read  and  contents  noted, 
and  therefore,  the  advantage  of  the  personal 
letter  over  the  ordinary  printed  circular  is 
apparent,  as  the  latter,  nine  cases  out  of  ten 
go  direct  to  the  waste  basket,  unread. 

By  my  patented  process,  of  which  this  is 
a  sample,  I  can  reproduce  any  number  of  copies  of 
a  type-written  or  pen-written  letter,  so  like  the 
original  as  to  defy  detection,  having  individual 
name  and  address  on  each  letter, at  a  cost  less  thai 
ordinary  printed  circulars.   I  am  also  prepared 
to  supply, print  and  address  envelopes  or  wrappers, 
as  well  as  letter-headings  or  circulars,  to  fold, 
enclose,  seal  and  stamp  same,  in  fact  provide 
letters  complete  for  mailing,  thus  obviating  the 
inconvenience  of  any  of  the  detail  work  to  adver- 
tiser. 

I  have  specially  compiled  lists  for  the 
different  trades,  as  well  as  65,000  desirable 
residents  of  New  York  and  Brooklyn. 

Send  for  samples  and  particulars. 
Yours  truly,

WHAT  OTHERS   HAVE  TO  SAY 


"The  results  from  Hall's  circulars  have  been  phenomenal.  In  a  certain  department 
where  we  once  had  a  revenue  of  from  $3.00  to  $9.00  a  day,  \ve  have  worked  up  same  to  from 
$25.00  to  $50.00  a  day — this  in  one  department  alone." 

— THE  ELECTRICAL  ENGINEER,  150  B'way,   N.  Y.  C 

"  The  circular  letters  yon  have  gotten  out  for  us  have  in  every  case  given  the  best  results. 
We  have  tried  everything  in  the  advertising  line  and  consider  your  system  the  best  we  have 
ever  tried."— CAMI-DELL  PRINTING  PRESS  &  MFG.  Co.,  i  Madison  Ave.,  X.  Y.  City. 

"  We  are  much  pleased  with  your  work  and  think  that  returns  from  your  letters  have  been 
ten  times  that  of  former  circulars  of  other  kinds." 

— THOMAS    KELLY,    PUBLISHER,    104  W.  i-jth  St.,  X.  Y. 

"  We  find  fully  500  per  cent,  more  replies  to  a  circular  printed  in  this  novel  style  and 
written  like  a  letter,  than  we  have  been  able  to  obtain  by  any  previous  method.  We  are 
pleased  to  assure  you  of  this  fact." 

— HENRY    HOPKINS   &   Co.,    PUBLISHERS,  99  Reade  St..    X.    Y.    City. 

"  We  do  not  believe  in  sending  the  ordinary  circulars  out  as  an  advertising  medium,  but  do 
believe  in  advertising  in  the  way  you  recommend.  *  *  *  Most  of  the  circulars  that  come 
to  us  we  throw  in  the  waste  basket ;  but  a  letter  or  something  that  has  a  close  resemblance  to 
a  letter,  we  take  the  trouble  to  read,  as  we  did  yours." 

—AM.  HARD  FIURE  COMPANY,  J.  F.  Quigley,  Pres.,  Newark,  Delaware,  U.  S.  A.

"  It  is  either  type-written  or  produced  in  such  close  imitation  of  type  writing  as  not  to  be 
distinguishable  therefrom." — C.  W.  DAYTON,  P.  M.,  X.  Y.  City.

XV111 


THOROUGH  THEORETICAL  and  PRACTICAL 

TRAINING  FOR  ASSOCIATION  WORK 


IS  PKOVIUED  BY 


THE  YOUNG  MEN'S  CHRISTIAN  ASSOCIATION  TRAINING  SCHOOL, 

IT_il_,. 


Western  Secretarial  Institute  of  the  Young  Men's  Christian 
Associations,  Lake  Geneva,  Wis. 

The  Training  School  was  Established  and  Incorporated  in  June,  1890,  and 

endorsed  as  an  INTERNATIONAL  TRAINING  SCHOOL  by  the  International 

Convention,  at  its  meeting  in  Kansas  City,  May,  1891. 

OBJECT. 

To  educate  young  men  for  the  duties  of  the  General  Secretaryship,  Physical  Directorship, 
Educational  Diiectorsbip  and  other  Association  offices. 

COURSES  OF  STUDY. 

The  complete  courses  cover  two  years,  and  compiise  in  the  Secretarial,  Physical  and 
Educational  Departments  :  First  —  Thorough  and  systematic  courses  of  study,  covering  every 
phase  of  Association  work.  Second—  A  practical  training,  each  student  being  assigned  to 
regular  duties  in  one  of  the  ten  departments  of  the  Chicago  Association.  Third—  A.  compre- 
hensive study  of  the  Bible,  and  how  to  use  and  teach  it.  Fourth—  Instruction  in  the  conduct 
ot  the  Bible  Training  Class  and  how  to  do  personal  work.  Fijth—  Daily  instruction  and 
practice  jn  gymnastics.  Sixth  —  Courses  in  the  work  of  the  Educa- 
tional Department  in  Christian  Sociology  and  lectures  on  general 
topics  closely  allied  to  Association  work. 

UNSURPASSED  EQUIPMENT. 

The  school  is  now  located  in  the  elegant  new  Central  Building 
i'f  the  Chicago  Association,  where  it  has  the  use  of  ample  class 
rooms,  good  library  facilities,  and  the  finest  Association  physical 
department  on  this  continent  This  greatly  adds  to  the  efficiency 
<»f  the  school,  and  it  gives  model  facilities  for  the  training  of  men 
for  Association  work. 

CALENDAR  SEVENTH  SCHOOL  YEAR. 

TALL  TERM-  Begins  Wednesday  morning,  September  9th,  1896. 
WINTER  TERM—  Begins  Wednesday  morning,  January  6tb,  1897 
SPRING  TERM—  Begins  Wednesday  morning,  March  31st,  1897. 

ESTIMATED  COST  FOR  SCHOOL  YEAR. 

Tuition,  $50.  Living  Expenses,  including  Board,  Room,  Asso- 
ciation Membership,  Gymnasium  Suits,  Laundry,  Text  Books  and 
attendance  upon  Conventions,  estimated  at  $185  to  $250. 

OFFICERS  AND  PRINCIPALS. 

ARTHUR  D.  WHEELER,  PRESIDENT.  SELDEN  P.  SPENCER,  VICE-PKESIDENT. 

H.  M.  STARKEY,  M  D..  REC.  SECRETARY.  JOHN  W.  HANSEL.  GENERAL  SKCRETARY.

HISTORY  OF  THE 


wing  IPen's  Christian 


L.  L.  DOGGETT,   PH.D. 

sHIS  volume,   the    first   of  three    to  be   issued,  was 
prepared  during  two  years  of  study  in  Germany 
and    was  presented   as    a  thesis  to  the  faculty  of 
Leipsic  University  in  1895. 

It  is  both  a  popular  and  philosophical  treatment  of 
the  conditions  and  circumstances  leading  to  the  organ- 
ization of  the  first  Association,  and  of  the  development  of 
the  work  to  the  year  1855. 


"  The  best  statement  of  the  origin  and  early  development  of  the  Associations 
which  I  have  ever  read."  G.  N.   BIERCE. 

"  It  should  find  a  place  in  the  library  of  every  Association  worker,  sociologist 
and  student  of  church  history."  J.  T.  BOWNE. 

"  The  most  scholarly,  accurate  and  best  written  presentation    of  the  Associa- 
tion's life  ever  prepared."  G.   K.   SHURTLEFF. 

"  I   value  it   among  the   books    I  own  and   would   recommend  it  to  every 
Association  Secretary."  R.  C.   MORSE.
